title: Dialects: Use backticks to quote Impala identifiers
description:
`tbl()` fails on an Impala ODBC connection while discovering table fields. The generated query uses double quotes around its alias, which Impala rejects:

```r
library(DBI)
library(odbc)
library(dbplyr)

con <- dbConnect(odbc(), "Impala DSN")

tbl(con, in_schema("public_db", "example_table"))
```

Applying an Impala dialect that quotes identifiers with backticks lets `tbl()` discover the fields:

```r
dialect_impala <- function() {
  new_sql_dialect(
    "impala",
    quote_identifier = function(x) sql_quote(x, "`"),
    has_window_clause = TRUE
  )
}

con2 <- with_dialect(con, dialect_impala())
tbl(con2, in_schema("public_db", "example_table"))
```

This change makes `dialect_impala()` use backticks and updates the corresponding translation tests.

Basically copied from #1840 and the edits in #1854.

title: Add IBM DB2 backend
description:
# PR Title
Add IBM DB2 backend

# PR Description

Adds support for IBM DB2 databases with the following features:

- Uses `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` syntax (DB2 standard) instead of `LIMIT n`
- Double-quote identifier quoting (DB2/ANSI standard)
- Automatic detection for JDBC connections using `com.ibm.db2.*` drivers

This follows the same pattern as other database backends (Oracle, SQL Server, etc.) and integrates with the existing JDBC backend infrastructure from #1783.

Also adds `/scratch/` directory to `.gitignore` for developer convenience when working with personal test scripts and connection configurations.

## Example Usage

```r
library(dplyr)

# Via JDBC
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  RJDBC::JDBC("com.ibm.db2.jcc.DB2Driver", "db2jcc.jar"),
  "jdbc:db2://host:port/database",
  "user",
  "password"
)

# Via ODBC (if DB2Connection class is recognized)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  odbc::odbc(),
  driver = "IBM DB2 ODBC DRIVER",
  database = "mydb"
)

# dbplyr automatically uses DB2 dialect
tbl(con, "my_table") |> head(10)
# Generates: SELECT * FROM "my_table" FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY
```

## Testing

Tested with:
- Simulated tests using `dialect_db2()`
- Real DB2 database via JDBC connection
- All backend tests passing

---

**Note**: This is a minimal initial implementation focusing on the critical SQL syntax differences. Additional DB2-specific features (string functions, date functions, temporary tables, etc.) can be added in future PRs as needed.

title: Replace IIF() with CASE WHEN for Azure Synapse compatibility

- mssql_as_bit(): CAST(IIF(x, 1, 0) AS BIT) -> CAST(CASE WHEN x THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS BIT)

title: add support for `DISTINCT ON`
description:
This PR is a first draft to address https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-r/issues/384, and add support for the usage of "DISTINCT ON" when using `distinct(..., .keep_all = TRUE)` which is a SQL variant supported by PostgreSQL, and DuckDB, see e.g. https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/query_syntax/select.html#distinct-on-clause. Currently, `.keep_all = TRUE` is implemented using window functions. Using `DISTINCT ON` instead promises a performance boost of that operation.

I came to the conclusion that this cannot be addressed within an external dbplyr backend, but it requires a minor modification of the `lazy_select_query` data structure itself:
Currently, a `lazy_select_query` supports a `distinct` state, which can be either `TRUE` or `FALSE` (corresponding to a normal `SELECT` vs. a `SELECT DISTINCT`.
The basic idea of this PR is to add a third state to the `distinct` attribute which represents a list of columns that belong to the `SELECT DISTICT ON (...)` clause.
Dbplyr backends can opt in to make use of `DISTINCT ON` via implementing a method of the new generic `supports_distinct_on()` that returns `TRUE`.

### Open issues

1. A major issue is the handling of the order specification. `DISTINCT ON` uses `ORDER BY` to specify an ordering. That is also a reason why `ORDER BY` is allowed in subqueries in PostgreSQL and DuckDB. As far as I can see, dbplyr currently forbids the `ORDER BY` statement in subqueries. I did not investigate yet, if that can be modified easily, or even can be changed at all. In any case, from the user-perspective `window_order()` would probably still be the right verb to specify the order.
2. The syntax highlighting of the currently generated SQL code is incorrect, that's probably because `sql_clause()` is not used correctly.
3. Having one `distinct` attribute that holds either `TRUE`, `FALSE` or a column list representation leads to a lot of required case distinction checks in the code, which are rather unpleasent to read and complicate the code. There is probably a way to model this in a more streamlined fashion.

I would appreciate feedback to the open issues as well as the already existing code. It might not be the right approach after all.

title: mutate() now supports the argument .keep = "transmute"
description:
Hi @hadley and @DavisVaughan,

This merge request seeks to support the new .keep = "transmute" argument in the mutate, based on the dplyr pull request   https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/pull/7038

Below I leave an example comparing transmute with mutate(.keep = "transmute")

```
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")

example <- tibble(
  group = c("a", "a", "b", "b"),
  old = c(1, 2, 3, 4)
)

example <- copy_to(con, example)

# transmute --------------------------------------------------------------------

example %>% transmute(
  group,
  new = old * 2,
  old
) %>% 
  show_query()

# <SQL>
SELECT `group`, `old` * 2.0 AS `new`, `old`
FROM `example`

# mutate(.keep = "transmute") --------------------------------------------------

example %>% mutate(
  .keep = "transmute",
  group,
  new = old * 2,
  old
) %>% 
  show_query()

# <SQL>
SELECT `group`, `old` * 2.0 AS `new`, `old`
FROM `example`

# group_by + transmute ---------------------------------------------------------

example %>% 
  group_by(group) %>% 
  transmute(
    new = sum(old,na.rm = TRUE),
    old
  ) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  show_query()

# <SQL>
SELECT `group`, SUM(`old`) OVER (PARTITION BY `group`) AS `new`, `old`
FROM `example`

# group_by + mutate(.keep = "transmute") ---------------------------------------

example %>% 
  group_by(group) %>% 
  mutate(
    .keep = "transmute",
    new = sum(old,na.rm = TRUE),
    old
  ) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  show_query()

# <SQL>
SELECT `group`, SUM(`old`) OVER (PARTITION BY `group`) AS `new`, `old`
FROM `example`

# mutate(.keep = "transmute", by = ...) ----------------------------------------

example %>%  
  mutate(
    .keep = "transmute",
    .by = "group",
    new = sum(old,na.rm = TRUE),
    old
  ) %>% 
  show_query()

# <SQL>
SELECT `group`, SUM(`old`) OVER (PARTITION BY `group`) AS `new`, `old`
FROM `example`
```

Regards,

title: Add "Supported By Posit" badge to website

## Overview

This PR adds the "Supported by Posit" badge to the website.

## Background

We've recently started adding a "Supported by Posit" badge across all Posit package websites to create a more cohesive brand presence. The badge appears on the far right of the top navigation bar or at the bottom of the hamburger menu. It links to Posit’s main website. @hadley is involved with this initiative.

The following websites already have the "Supported by Posit" badge: [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org), [Great Tables](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/articles/intro.html), [gt](https://gt.rstudio.com), [Plotnine](https://plotnine.org), [Pointblank](https://posit-dev.github.io/pointblank/), [pointblank](https://rstudio.github.io/pointblank/), and [Quarto](https://quarto.org).

See https://posit-dev.github.io/supported-by-posit/ for more information.

## Changes

- Added a line to `_pkgdown.yml` to include the JavaScript file
- Standardized indentation in `_pkgdown.yml`

title: Simplify escaping strategy
description:
The big idea in this PR is to simplify the implementation by immediately escaping as soon as we get a table name. That allows user facing functions to accept a wide range of table specifications while internal functions only need to deal with a new `table_name` class. Additionally, only the `table_name` class is vectorised, so we can ensure that user supplies a single table name (or SQL, where appropriate), while still providing vectorised tools internally. Since we escape table ids early we also need a new tool to extract the name of just the table; this is sort of the opposite problem to `table_ident` which needed tools to stitch components together instead of pulling them apart.

I've also simplified the implementation a little by taking `I()` to mean "don't escape". My expectation is that `I("foo.bar")`/`I("foo.bar.baz"))` will become the preferred way to specify nested tables.

title: Filtering for MS SQL Consistent with dplyr
description:
Fixes #1233 boolean translation issue

This PR would make MS SQL filtering behavior more consistent with dplyr/other databases. Currently, filter expressions with a symbol or atomic value that aren't a part of a logical expression will fail.

Both of these queries will fail because the WHERE clauses are invalid in T-SQL. The values must be a part of a comparison expression (e.g. 1 == 1).
``` r
tbl(con, "mtcars") |> filter(TRUE) |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT "mtcars".*
#> FROM "mtcars"
#> WHERE (1)

tbl(con, "mtcars") |> mutate(x = mpg < 15) |> filter(x) |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT "q01".*
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT "mtcars".*, CAST(IIF("mpg" < 15.0, 1, 0) AS BIT) AS "x"
#>   FROM "mtcars"
#> ) "q01"
#> WHERE ("x")
```

The general strategy of the PR is to examine all of the WHERE clauses of a query and look for:

+ Top level atoms/symbols (as above)
+ Atoms/symbols involved in an expression that would require a logical (e.g. `|`)

When either of these are found the values are explicitly cast and made part of an equality expression. All other expressions remain as-is.

``` r
tbl(con, "mtcars") |> filter(TRUE) |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT "mtcars".*
#> FROM "mtcars"
#> WHERE (cast(1 AS "BIT") = 1)

tbl(con, "mtcars") |> mutate(x = mpg < 15) |> filter(x) |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT "q01".*
#> FROM (
#>   SELECT "mtcars".*, CAST(IIF("mpg" < 15.0, 1, 0) AS BIT) AS "x"
#>   FROM "mtcars"
#> ) "q01"
#> WHERE (cast("x" AS "BIT") = 1)

tbl(con, "mtcars") |> filter(FALSE | TRUE | TRUE == TRUE) |> show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT "mtcars".*
#> FROM "mtcars"
#> WHERE (cast(0 AS "BIT") = 1 OR cast(1 AS "BIT") = 1 OR 1 = 1)
```

title: Multiple joins in one query
description:
Closes #865. This PR replaces #894.

The code currently has some rough edges that still need to be improved. One has to be quite careful when a series of `left/inner_join()` can be done in a single query but it produces much nicer queries in the end.

## Remarks
* For simplicity, I just used `vec_as_names()` to produce unique names. We might want something else? I just remembered that we considered using `abbreviate()`. I'll take a look at that in another PR.
* The `lazy_join_query` structure is basically not needed in this our codebase anymore. It would make sense to remove it but as it is exported I wanted to check whether it is in use somewhere or not.

## Names for Subqueries

```r
lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 1)

left_join(
  lf %>% filter(x == 1),
  lf %>% filter(a > 1),
  by = "x"
)
```

Produces

```sql
SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `LHS`.`a` AS `a.x`, `RHS`.`a` AS `a.y`
FROM (
  SELECT *
  FROM `df`
  WHERE (`x` = 1.0)
) `LHS`
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT *
  FROM `df`
  WHERE (`a` > 1.0)
) `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```

## Self-Join

```r
lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 1)

left_join(
  lf,
  lf,
  by = "x"
)
```

```sql
SELECT `df_LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `df_LHS`.`a` AS `a.x`, `df_RHS`.`a` AS `a.y`
FROM `df` AS `df_LHS`
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df_RHS`
  ON (`df_LHS`.`x` = `df_RHS`.`x`)
```

## User Provided Alias

```r
left_join(
  lf,
  lf,
  by = "x",
  x_as = "df"
) %>% 
  left_join(lf, by = "x")
```

The alias provided by the user always wins. So this produces

```sql
SELECT
  `df`.`x` AS `x`,
  `df`.`a` AS `a.x`,
  `df...2`.`a` AS `a.y`,
  `df...3`.`a` AS `a`
FROM `df`
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...2`
  ON (`df`.`x` = `df...2`.`x`)
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...3`
  ON (`df`.`x` = `df...3`.`x`)
```

Note that an alias for `x` can also be provided later on. So, this produces the same query:

```r
left_join(
  lf,
  lf,
  by = "x"
) %>% 
  left_join(lf, by = "x", x_as = "df")
```

## Conflicting Alias

In case of a conflicting alias a subquery is used

```r
left_join(
  lf,
  lf,
  x_as = "df",
  by = "x"
) %>% 
  left_join(lf, by = "x", x_as = "df2")
```

```sql
SELECT `df2`.*, `a`
FROM (
  SELECT `df`.`x` AS `x`, `df`.`a` AS `a.x`, `df...2`.`a` AS `a.y`
  FROM `df`
  LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...2`
    ON (`df`.`x` = `df...2`.`x`)
) `df2`
LEFT JOIN `df`
  ON (`df2`.`x` = `df`.`x`)
```

I expected the same treatment for the `db_collect` generic, but the ellipsis is missing in the `collect.tbl_sql` function: https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/main/R/verb-compute.R#L122

This PR fixes this issue by adding the missing ellipsis to the call to `db_collect` from the `collect.tbl_sql()` so that `db_collect` behaves in much the same way as `db_compute` and `db_copy_to`.

The reason I am interested in this is that I have implemented a DBI backend for a proprietary database, and this database is capable of natively representing/coercing (some) data in a variety of different types. As a result, we have added an extra argument to our `dbFetch` DBI method called `colClasses` that can be used to explicitly set what R types should be used for the result data frame columns. This works, but there does not appear to be any way to pass this argument through dbplyr.

After applying the change in this PR I believe we should be able to do this by using an explicit call to `collect()`:

For example:
```
tbl %>% collect(colClasses=c("character", "integer"))
```

title: Add <dbplyr_table_ident>
description:
Currently, there are multiple classes that can be used to create a sql tbl:

* `<ident>`
* `<dbplyr_schema>`
* `<dbplyr_catalog>`
* `<Id> (from DBI)`
* `<sql>`
* `<SQL>`

This is quite messy, needs lots of testing and lots of extra code to support every case. Further, these classes have some annoying properties (e.g. see #1205). This PR improves the situation by adding a new class <dbplyr_table_ident> which replaces these classes (at least internally for now).

Its using `vctrs::rcrd()` under the hood. In most cases we don't really need (or want) anything but a single table but it might still be nice to have the vector properties.

There are a couple of questions though:

1. `in_schema()` and `in_catalog()` support <ident_q>, e.g. `in_schema(ident_q("a b"), "table")` gives `` <SCHEMA> a b.`table` ``. I don't think it is used often and I don't really see the need for it. Supporting this would make the implementation more complicated.
2. Should we deprecate `<dbplyr_schema>` and `<dbplyr_catalog>`? We use it internally anyway, so package authors might need to adapt to it anyway. Also, they would likely face the same issues we had with the schema and catalog classes.
3. I would love to get rid of the `sql` field in the table ident class. Unfortunately, it is needed to support `<ident_q>`. Could we deprecate `<ident_q>` for table identifiers? I don't really see a good use case for them. I think they rather make problems than provide actual benefit.


Closes #1204. Closes #1205. Closes #1261. Closes #1139. Closes #1264.

title: Add argument `use_star`
description:
Part of #1146.

``` r
lf1 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 2, z = 2, .name = "df1")
lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 2, b = 2, .name = "df2")

left_join_lf <- left_join(lf1, lf2, by = "x")
left_join_lf %>% show_query(use_star = TRUE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `df1`.*, `a`, `b`
#> FROM `df1`
#> LEFT JOIN `df2`
#>   ON (`df1`.`x` = `df2`.`x`)
left_join_lf %>% show_query(use_star = FALSE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `df1`.`x` AS `x`, `y`, `z`, `a`, `b`
#> FROM `df1`
#> LEFT JOIN `df2`
#>   ON (`df1`.`x` = `df2`.`x`)

right_join_lf <- right_join(lf1, lf2, by = "x") %>% select(x, a, b, y, z)
right_join_lf %>% show_query(use_star = TRUE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `df2`.*, `y`, `z`
#> FROM `df1`
#> RIGHT JOIN `df2`
#>   ON (`df1`.`x` = `df2`.`x`)
right_join_lf %>% show_query(use_star = FALSE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `df2`.`x` AS `x`, `a`, `b`, `y`, `z`
#> FROM `df1`
#> RIGHT JOIN `df2`
#>   ON (`df1`.`x` = `df2`.`x`)

cross_join_lf <- cross_join(lf1, lf2 %>% select(-x))
cross_join_lf %>% show_query(use_star = TRUE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `df1`.*, `a`, `b`
#> FROM `df1`
#> CROSS JOIN `df2`
cross_join_lf %>% show_query(use_star = FALSE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `df1`.`x` AS `x`, `y`, `z`, `a`, `b`
#> FROM `df1`
#> CROSS JOIN `df2`

semi_join_lf <- semi_join(lf1, lf2, by = "x")
semi_join_lf %>% show_query(use_star = TRUE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *
#> FROM `df1`
#> WHERE EXISTS (
#>   SELECT 1 FROM `df2`
#>   WHERE (`df1`.`x` = `df2`.`x`)
#> )
semi_join_lf %>% show_query(use_star = FALSE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x`, `y`, `z`
#> FROM `df1`
#> WHERE EXISTS (
#>   SELECT 1 FROM `df2`
#>   WHERE (`df1`.`x` = `df2`.`x`)
#> )

mutate_lf <- lf1 %>% mutate(a = 1)
mutate_lf %>% show_query(use_star = TRUE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT *, 1.0 AS `a`
#> FROM `df1`
mutate_lf %>% show_query(use_star = FALSE)
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT `x`, `y`, `z`, 1.0 AS `a`
#> FROM `df1`
```

title: Multiple joins in one query
description:
Closes #865.

One has to be quite careful when a series of `left/inner_join()` can be done in a single query but it produces much nicer queries in the end.

## Remarks
* For simplicity, I just used `vec_as_names()` to produce unique names. We might want something else? I just remembered that we considered using `abbreviate()`. I'll take a look at that in another PR.
* The `lazy_join_query` structure is basically not needed in this our codebase anymore. It would make sense to remove it but as it is exported I wanted to check whether it is in use somewhere or not.

## Names for Subqueries

```r
lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 1)

left_join(
  lf %>% filter(x == 1),
  lf %>% filter(a > 1),
  by = "x"
)
```

Produces

```sql
SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `LHS`.`a` AS `a.x`, `RHS`.`a` AS `a.y`
FROM (
  SELECT *
  FROM `df`
  WHERE (`x` = 1.0)
) `LHS`
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT *
  FROM `df`
  WHERE (`a` > 1.0)
) `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```

## Self-Join

```r
lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 1)

left_join(
  lf,
  lf,
  by = "x"
)
```

```sql
SELECT `df_LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `df_LHS`.`a` AS `a.x`, `df_RHS`.`a` AS `a.y`
FROM `df` AS `df_LHS`
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df_RHS`
  ON (`df_LHS`.`x` = `df_RHS`.`x`)
```

## User Provided Alias

```r
left_join(
  lf,
  lf,
  by = "x",
  x_as = "df"
) %>% 
  left_join(lf, by = "x")
```

The alias provided by the user always wins. So this produces

```sql
SELECT
  `df`.`x` AS `x`,
  `df`.`a` AS `a.x`,
  `df...2`.`a` AS `a.y`,
  `df...3`.`a` AS `a`
FROM `df`
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...2`
  ON (`df`.`x` = `df...2`.`x`)
LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...3`
  ON (`df`.`x` = `df...3`.`x`)
```

Note that an alias for `x` can also be provided later on. So, this produces the same query:

```r
left_join(
  lf,
  lf,
  by = "x"
) %>% 
  left_join(lf, by = "x", x_as = "df")
```

## Conflicting Alias

In case of a conflicting alias a subquery is used

```r
left_join(
  lf,
  lf,
  x_as = "df",
  by = "x"
) %>% 
  left_join(lf, by = "x", x_as = "df2")
```

```sql
SELECT `df2`.*, `a`
FROM (
  SELECT `df`.`x` AS `x`, `df`.`a` AS `a.x`, `df...2`.`a` AS `a.y`
  FROM `df`
  LEFT JOIN `df` AS `df...2`
    ON (`df`.`x` = `df...2`.`x`)
) `df2`
LEFT JOIN `df`
  ON (`df2`.`x` = `df`.`x`)
```

title: Only use table alias in joins if necessary
description:
A bit more work than expected due to some edge cases:

1. `left_join(x, x)` still need a table alias. The question is whether they should both use an alias or only one of the tables?
2. `left_join(x, y, sql_on = ...)` should still use the table alias `LHS` and `RHS` to not be a breaking change

In some cases the error message might not be helpful but I think this is mostly in edge cases so I didn't want to put in too much effort for now.

```r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 1, .name = "df1")
lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, b = 2, .name = "df2")

left_join(lf, lf2, by = "x")
```

Before

```sql
SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `a`, `b`
FROM `df1` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `df2` AS `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```

After

```sql
SELECT `df1`.`x` AS `x`, `a`, `b`
FROM `df1`
LEFT JOIN `df2`
  ON (`df1`.`x` = `df2`.`x`)
```

```r
lf %>% 
  filter(a == 1) %>% 
  left_join(lf2, by = "x")
```

Before

```sql
SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `a`, `b`
FROM (
  SELECT *
  FROM `df1`
  WHERE (`a` = 1.0)
) `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `df2` AS `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```

After

```sql
SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `a`, `b`
FROM (
  SELECT *
  FROM `df1`
  WHERE (`a` = 1.0)
) `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `df2`
  ON (`LHS`.`x` = `df2`.`x`)
```

``` r
lf2 <- lazy_frame(a = 1, a1 = 1, a2 = 1)

lf1 |>
```

title: Inline `select()` after `*_join()`
description:
Closes #866.

``` r
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf1 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, a = 1, .name = "lf1")
lf2 <- lazy_frame(x = 1, b = 2, .name = "lf2")
```

`left/right/full/inner_join()`

```r
left_join(lf1, lf2, by = "x") %>%
  select(b, x)
```

before

```sql
SELECT `b`, `x`
FROM (
  SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `a`, `b`
  FROM `lf1` AS `LHS`
  LEFT JOIN `lf2` AS `RHS`
    ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
) `q01`
```

after

```sql
SELECT `b`, `LHS`.`x` AS `x`
FROM `lf1` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `lf2` AS `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```

`semi/anti_join()`

```r
semi_join(lf1, lf2, by = "x") %>%
  select(x)
```

Before

```sql
SELECT `x`
FROM (
  SELECT * FROM `lf1` AS `LHS`
  WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM `lf2` AS `RHS`
    WHERE (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
  )
) `q01`
```

After

```sql
SELECT `x`
FROM `lf1` AS `LHS`
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM `lf2` AS `RHS`
  WHERE (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
)
```

<sup>Created on 2022-05-18 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

For `semi/anti_join()` this only works with projections (i.e. `select()` and `rename()`). In the long run one could merge `lazy_semi_join_query()` and `lazy_select_query()` as `semi_join()` and `anti_join()` are simply translated to `WHERE (NOT) EXISTS`. But I'd keep them separate for now and explore that at a different time.

description:

```r
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

lf2 <- lazy_frame(x2 = 10, b = 2, z = 4, .name = "lf2")
```

```r
  lf %>% select(a2 = a, x = x1),

  by = "x"
```

```sql
SELECT `a2`, `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `b`
FROM (
  SELECT `a` AS `a2`, `x1` AS `x`
  FROM `lf1`
) `LHS`
```

```sql
FROM `lf1` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `lf2` AS `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`x1` = `RHS`.`x2`)
```

`semi/anti_join()`

```r
semi_join(
  lf %>% select(a2 = a, x = x1),
  lf2 %>% select(x = x2, b),
  by = "x"
)
```

Before

```sql
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT `a` AS `a2`, `x1` AS `x`
  FROM `lf1`
) `LHS`
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM (
  SELECT `x2` AS `x`, `b`
  FROM `lf2`
) `RHS`
  WHERE (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
)
```

After

```sql

FROM `lf1` AS `LHS`
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM (
  SELECT `x2` AS `x`, `b`
  FROM `lf2`
) `RHS`
  WHERE (`LHS`.`x1` = `RHS`.`x`)
```

title: Lazy render pipeline
description:
This is the first PR of optimising the render pipe line and producing shorter SQL.
The goals of this PR are:

* do not change the generated SQL
* use "lazy queries" instead of `op` objects for rendering
* only convert R code to SQL when it is actually necessary, i.e. when the user `collect()`s or uses `show_query()`

The PR is quite big as basically every verb has to be touched. I remove all the code around `op` object. We could also keep it for a while so that the user can switch back to the "old" pipeline via an option (this can easily be done in `sql_render.tbl_lazy()`). Also this might break some packages (e.g. `sparklyr` currently uses it in some places).

## Overview
A lazy table now stores a nested list of "lazy queries" in its field "lazy_query". The lazy queries do not store SQL code but all the information necessary to generate the correct SQL. There are six lazy queries:

* `lazy_query_local` and `lazy_query_remote` are the equivalent of `op_base_*`. They are used to store the information about a local resp. database table.
* `lazy_select_query`, `lazy_join_query`, `lazy_semi_join_query`, and `lazy_set_op_query` are the lazy versions of `select_query` etc. The last three are actually (currently) identical to their non-lazy counterparts because the non-lazy versions already do not store SQL.

The `lazy_select_query` has the following fields similar to `select_query`

* `from`: a lazy query
* `select`: a tibble with the following columns
  * `name`: output name (string) of the column
  * `expr`: a quosure or an expression describing the expression for the output column
  * `group_vars`: a character string describing the grouping variables in case `expr` has a window function
  * `order_vars`: a quosure or an expressions describing the ordering expressions in case `expr` has a window function
  * `frame`: two integerish numbers describing the frame in case `expr` has a window function
* `where`: an unnamed list of quosures
* `group_by`
  * an unnamed list of symbols
  * this could use quosures in the future to allow inline some code
* `order_by`
  * an unnamed list of quosures
* `distinct`: if `TRUE` use `SELECT DISTINCT`
* `limit`: number of rows to return

and the following additional fields
* `last_op`: the most recent applied operation; this is (currently) needed for optimisations in `mutate()`, `select()`, and `head()`
* `group_vars`: current grouping vars; an unnamed list of symbols
* `group_order`: current ordering vars; an unnamed list of quosures
* `frame`: current frame; two integerish numbers
* `select_operation`: either `"mutate"` or `"summarise"`. This is needed to know how to generate the SQL code in the `SELECT` clause
* `message_summarise`: needed to inform about new groups after `summarise()`

## Next Steps
* `sql_optimise()` removes unnecessary variables from subqueries
* `filter()` checks if it can avoid adding a new query
* `mutate()`/`transmute()` check if it can avoid adding a new query. This should use an improved `get_mutate_layers()` from #671.
* Use `HAVING` clause
* Applying a verb on a join does not result in a new query (i.e. actually use the `SELECT` clause etc after a join)

## Notes
* In `test-verb-arrange.R` there is the following test

```r
"warn if arrange before join"
lf %>% arrange(a) %>% left_join(rf)
lf %>% arrange(a) %>% semi_join(rf)
lf %>% arrange(a) %>% union(rf)
```

The last test with `union()` did not produce a warning before and does not do it now

* In some cases multiple `arrange()`s seem to combine, in others not. I think they should not combine but this should be clarified. Also see https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/pull/672

* Fixed a bug where columns dropped with `NULL` where still appeared in `op_vars`

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

lazy_frame(x = 1, y = 1) %>%
  mutate(y = NULL) %>% 
  op_vars()
#> [1] "x" "y"
```

title: Use CTE
description:
Closes #638.

I hacked together the support for CTE. Adding CTEs to `dbplyr` definitely seems doable. Together with [custom join aliases](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/pull/637) this would greatly improve readability.

There might be some limitations where CTEs cannot be used or where this implementation doesn't work. Therefore, I added a parameter `cte` so the user can decide whether to use CTE clauses or not. I'd propose to not use CTEs by default (at least for now) and see whether things work fine. It might be worth to use an option as default value.

Some notes

* rendering the CTEs needs to be done in the first function calling `sql_render()` due to the "branching" in join and set op queries.
* In `sql_render()` for `select_query`, `set_op_query`, `join_query`, `semi_join_query` we need to register the subqueries and give them names. This is currently done via passing a list.
* Currently, it is quite a hack how the four functions above know about `cte = TRUE`. It would probably be nicer to pass `cte` explicitly but I had the feeling that quite a lot of functions would need to know about it and pass it along. I'll check again later if this is doable or not.
* It would be nice if one could use custom names for the CTEs but this comes with a couple of questions (we probably need more subqueries than the user anticipates; what if the user specifies a name but the next step could also be included to generate the sql; ...)

``` r
devtools::load_all("~/GitHub/dbplyr/")

flights_db <- tbl_memdb(nycflights13::flights)
airports_db <- tbl_memdb(nycflights13::airports)
```

## Example for select query

``` r
select_query <- flights_db %>% 
  group_by(dest) %>% 
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    dist = mean(distance, na.rm = TRUE),
    delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>% 
  filter(delay, count > 20, dest != "HNL")
```

```sql
-- show_query(select_query, cte = TRUE)
WITH `q01` AS (
SELECT `dest`, COUNT(*) AS `count`, AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`, AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
FROM `nycflights13::flights`
GROUP BY `dest`
)
SELECT *
FROM `q01`
WHERE ((`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL'))

-- show_query(select_query, cte = FALSE)
SELECT *
FROM (SELECT `dest`, COUNT(*) AS `count`, AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`, AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
FROM `nycflights13::flights`
GROUP BY `dest`)
WHERE ((`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL'))
```

## Example for join query

```r
join_query <- left_join(
  select_query,
  airports_db %>% 
    select(faa, name, tzone),
  by = c(dest = "faa")
)
```

```sql
-- show_query(join_query, cte = TRUE)
<SQL>
WITH `q01` AS (
SELECT `dest`, COUNT(*) AS `count`, AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`, AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
FROM `nycflights13::flights`
GROUP BY `dest`
),
`q02` AS (
SELECT *
FROM `q01`
WHERE ((`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL'))
),
`q03` AS (
SELECT `faa`, `name`, `tzone`
FROM `nycflights13::airports`
)
SELECT `dest`, `count`, `dist`, `delay`, `name`, `tzone`
FROM `q02` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `q03` AS `RHS`
ON (`LHS`.`dest` = `RHS`.`faa`)

-- show_query(join_query, cte = FALSE)
<SQL>
SELECT `dest`, `count`, `dist`, `delay`, `name`, `tzone`
FROM (SELECT *
FROM (SELECT `dest`, COUNT(*) AS `count`, AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`, AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
FROM `nycflights13::flights`
GROUP BY `dest`)
WHERE ((`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL'))) AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN (SELECT `faa`, `name`, `tzone`
FROM `nycflights13::airports`) AS `RHS`
ON (`LHS`.`dest` = `RHS`.`faa`)
```

## Reuse CTE

``` r
union(
  select_query,
  select_query
) %>% 
  show_query(cte = TRUE)
```

```sql
WITH `q01` AS (
SELECT `dest`, COUNT(*) AS `count`, AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`, AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
FROM `nycflights13::flights`
GROUP BY `dest`
),
`q02` AS (
SELECT *
FROM `q01`
WHERE ((`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL'))
)
SELECT *
FROM `q02`
UNION
SELECT *
FROM `q02`
```

title: Support CTE
description:
Closes #638.

It was easier to create a new PR than to deal with all the merge conflicts in the old PR.
Thanks to the lazy query approach merged, the support for CTEs is now quite simple.

``` r
devtools::load_all("~/GitHub/dbplyr/")

flights_db <- tbl_memdb(nycflights13::flights)
airports_db <- tbl_memdb(nycflights13::airports)
```

## Example for select query

``` r
select_query <- flights_db %>% 
  group_by(dest) %>% 
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    dist = mean(distance, na.rm = TRUE),
    delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>% 
  filter(delay, count > 20, dest != "HNL")
```

```sql
-- show_query(select_query, cte = TRUE)
WITH `q01` AS (
  SELECT
    `dest`,
    COUNT(*) AS `count`,
    AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`,
    AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
  FROM `nycflights13::flights`
  GROUP BY `dest`
)
SELECT *
FROM `q01`
WHERE (`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL')

-- show_query(select_query, cte = FALSE)
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT
    `dest`,
    COUNT(*) AS `count`,
    AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`,
    AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
  FROM `nycflights13::flights`
  GROUP BY `dest`
)
WHERE (`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL')
```

## Example for join query

```r
join_query <- left_join(
  select_query,
  airports_db %>% 
    select(faa, name, tzone),
  by = c(dest = "faa")
)
```

```sql
-- show_query(join_query, cte = TRUE)
WITH `q01` AS (
  SELECT
    `dest`,
    COUNT(*) AS `count`,
    AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`,
    AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
  FROM `nycflights13::flights`
  GROUP BY `dest`
),
`q02` AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM `q01`
  WHERE (`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL')
),
`q03` AS (
  SELECT `faa`, `name`, `tzone`
  FROM `nycflights13::airports`
)
SELECT `dest`, `count`, `dist`, `delay`, `name`, `tzone`
FROM `q02` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `q03` AS `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`dest` = `RHS`.`faa`)

-- show_query(join_query, cte = FALSE)
SELECT `dest`, `count`, `dist`, `delay`, `name`, `tzone`
FROM (
  SELECT *
  FROM (
    SELECT
      `dest`,
      COUNT(*) AS `count`,
      AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`,
      AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
    FROM `nycflights13::flights`
    GROUP BY `dest`
  )
  WHERE (`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL')
) AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT `faa`, `name`, `tzone`
  FROM `nycflights13::airports`
) AS `RHS`
  ON (`LHS`.`dest` = `RHS`.`faa`)
```

## Reuse CTE

``` r
union(
  select_query,
  select_query
) %>% 
  show_query(cte = TRUE)
```

```sql
WITH `q01` AS (
  SELECT
    `dest`,
    COUNT(*) AS `count`,
    AVG(`distance`) AS `dist`,
    AVG(`arr_delay`) AS `delay`
  FROM `nycflights13::flights`
  GROUP BY `dest`
),
`q02` AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM `q01`
  WHERE (`delay`) AND (`count` > 20.0) AND (`dest` != 'HNL')
)
SELECT *
FROM `q02`
UNION
SELECT *
FROM `q02`
```

title: Add `rows_*()` verbs
description:
Closes #736.

`returning`: This argument is still experimental and not (yet?) in the generic. ~To support `tidyselect` and not trigger a warning by `rlang::check_dots_used()` (in the generic) the user has to quote it manually (see https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5985).~ (Edit: not necessary anymore after `check_dots_used()` was removed in the generic).
Theoretically, one could execute arbitrary SQL in the `RETURNING` clause but I'm not sure whether there are sufficient use cases to support this.

`nonexistent`: The current implementation is `nonexistent = "ignore"`. To support `nonexistent = "error"` one could use a foreign key constraint on `y`. I'll tackle this in another PR. (Update: renamed to `unmatched` and "error" is not supported for now)

`rows_upsert()`: This is the most tricky and needs different methods:
* Some databases (e.g. Oracle or MS SQL) support `MERGE INTO ... WHEN (NOT) MATCHED`
* Some databases (e.g. SQLite, Postgres) have an upsert if there is a unique constraint, basically `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE/NOTHING`
* If there is no unique constraint this can still be done in one query with a CTE (e.g. Postgres) or two queries (e.g. SQLite)

It might make sense to add an argument so that the user can choose whether a unique constraint exists or not. See
https://github.com/cynkra/dm/pull/616#issuecomment-920613435 for some more information on the Pros/Cons. I will do this in another PR.

title: Named window expressions
description:
Fixes #624.
After I also wished for named windows a couple of times I had a first go at it. The idea is relatively simple:

In `sql_build.op_select()` have (possibly) two runs of translating the variables. In the first run `win_over()` registers every window it uses. After this first translation create a name for every window that is used more than once. Then translate the variables again but this time use the window name if one is available.

Example SQL

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

lf <- lazy_frame(
  col1 = runif(3),
  col2 = runif(3),
  col3 = runif(3),
  col4 = runif(3),
  part = c("a", "a", "b"),
  ord = 3:1
) %>% 
  group_by(part) %>% 
  window_order(ord)

# window only used once -> no need to name the window
lf %>% 
  mutate(
    across(c(col1), sum, na.rm = TRUE),
    across(c(col3), ~ order_by(desc(ord), cumsum(.x)))
  )
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT SUM(`col1`) OVER (PARTITION BY `part`) AS `col1`, `col2`, SUM(`col3`) OVER (PARTITION BY `part` ORDER BY `ord` DESC ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS `col3`, `col4`, `part`, `ord`
#> FROM `df`

lf %>% 
  mutate(
    across(c(col1, col2), sum, na.rm = TRUE),
    across(c(col3, col4), ~ order_by(desc(ord), cumsum(.x)))
  )
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT SUM(`col1`) OVER (`win1`) AS `col1`, SUM(`col2`) OVER (`win1`) AS `col2`, SUM(`col3`) OVER (`win2`) AS `col3`, SUM(`col4`) OVER (`win2`) AS `col4`, `part`, `ord`
#> FROM `df`
#> WINDOW `win1` AS (PARTITION BY `part`), `win2` AS (PARTITION BY `part` ORDER BY `ord` DESC ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
```

description:
Fixes #804

This pull request adds a Redshift specific translation to `str_flatten`. Currently the default Postgres translation (`string_agg`) is used, but it is not supported in Redshift. The equivalent function in Redshift is `LISTAGG` but it has a slightly different syntax (requires `WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...)` syntax for ordering).

Please check below the reprex with the expected output:

``` r
library(dbplyr)
library(DBI)
library(reprex)

con <- dbConnect(RPostgres::Redshift(), 
                 host = ,
                 dbname = , 
                 port = ,
                 user = , 
                 password = ) 

example_table <- dplyr::tribble(
  ~customer, ~day, ~item,
  "A", 1, "WATER",
  "A", 3, "BREAD",
  "A", 2, "JUICE",
  "B", 1, "APPLE",
  "B", 4, "BANANA",
  "C", 1, "MILK"
)

table_db <- dplyr::copy_to(con, example_table, temporary = T)

table_db %>%
  dplyr::group_by(customer) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(flat_string = str_flatten(item, "-"))
#> # Source:   [?? x 2]
#> # Database: postgres
#> #   []
#>   customer flat_string      
#>   <chr>    <chr>            
#> 1 B        APPLE-BANANA     
#> 2 C        MILK             
#> 3 A        WATER-BREAD-JUICE

table_db %>%
  dplyr::group_by(customer) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(flat_string = str_flatten(item, "-")) %>% 
  dplyr::show_query()
#> <SQL>
#> SELECT "customer", LISTAGG("item", '-') AS "flat_string"
#> FROM "example_table"
#> GROUP BY "customer"

table_db %>%
  dplyr::group_by(customer) %>%
  dbplyr::window_order(day) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(flat_string = str_flatten(item, "-")) 
#> # Source:     [?? x 4]
#> # Database:   postgres
#> #   []
#> # Groups:     customer
#> # Ordered by: day
#>   customer   day item   flat_string      
#>   <chr>    <dbl> <chr>  <chr>            
#> 1 A            1 WATER  WATER-JUICE-BREAD
#> 2 A            2 JUICE  WATER-JUICE-BREAD

#> 4 C            1 MILK   MILK

#> 6 B            4 BANANA APPLE-BANANA

  dplyr::group_by(customer) %>%
  dbplyr::window_order(day) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(flat_string = str_flatten(item, "-")) %>%
  dplyr::show_query()

#>   "day",
#>   "item",
```

title: Added missing connection parameter to the dbplyr_fill0 implementation
description:
The connection parameter was not passed to the first translate_sql() call in the dbplyr_fill0 implementation for databases without support for IGNORE NULLS. Because of that the quotes other than \`  \` were not correct for that particular translate_sql() call.

Following the example in the [fill documentation](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/fill.tbl_lazy.html) the produced SQL was as follows with a database that uses " " as quotes:

```sql
<SQL>
SELECT "group", "name", "role", MAX("n_squirrels") OVER (PARTITION BY "..dbplyr_partion_1") AS "n_squirrels", 
MAX("n_squirrels2") OVER (PARTITION BY "..dbplyr_partion_2") AS "n_squirrels2", "id" FROM
(SELECT "group", "name", "role", "n_squirrels", "n_squirrels2", "id", SUM(CASE WHEN (((`n_squirrels`) IS NULL)) THEN 0 
ELSE 1 END) OVER (ORDER BY "id" ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS "..dbplyr_partion_1", 
SUM(CASE WHEN (((`n_squirrels2`) IS NULL))  THEN 0 ELSE 1 END) OVER (ORDER BY "id" ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS
"..dbplyr_partion_2" FROM "squirrels") "q01"
```

So following the `SUM(CASE WHEN...` there are wrong quotes in two places (around the variable names).

The fix was simple and only requires that the missing connection parameter is added to the translate_sql() call as shown in the commit.

title: New render pipeline
description:
## Current Translation Approach

The translation currently consists of two stages:

1. The "operation" stage: Whenever a "basic" `dplyr` verb is applied to a lazy table it adds an operation describing the verb and its argument to the `ops` field of the lazy table. This quickly results in a deeply nested list.
2. `sql_build()` creates a query object (`select_query()`, `join_query`, `semi_join_query`, or `set_op_query`) which is a container containing SQL for e.g. `SELECT` or `WHERE`
3. `sql_optimise()` tries to combine the query objects generated in the previous step to generate less nested SQL
4. `sql_render()` converts the query objects to actual SQL for the corresponding backend

Issues with the approach:
* the operations list is quickly deeply nested resulting in a big call stack in `sql_build()`
* many optimisations cannot be applied anymore as it would require re-rendering the SQL generated in the previous step
* Things like using CTEs is a bit hacky


## New Approach

Replace the `ops` field by a `query_list` field. This `query_list` consists of "lazy" query objects which are similar to the current query objects but they are containers for quosures instead of containers for SQL.

The new pipe basically looks as follows:

1. Each "basic" `dplyr` verb adds a or modifies the current "lazy" query object to the `query_list` field of the lazy tables
2. `sql_optimise()` removes unnecessary variables, tries to merge query objects, and removes trivial ones
3. `sql_build()` iterates over `query_list` and translates the quosures to SQL. It produces the current query objects
4. `sql_render()` can stay unchanged.

This should allow to tackle the following issues
* #725 
* #722 
* #721 
* #719

And help in these PRs
* #656 
* #637

Overall, this should allow to produce much more natural SQL.

title: Indentation
description:
Fixes #636.

I am not sure what should be controllable via an option and what should be the new default. I think the following options make sense

* **base indent:** the base indent used; defaults to two spaces "  " but this could be any number of spaces or tabs
* **indent_strategy:** I added four strategies
  * `"legacy"`: produces the same output as `dbplyr` does currently
  * `"minimal"`: indent subqueries
  * `"indent"`: each field on its own line. Line break after keyword and fields are one level more intended than the keyword
```sql
SELECT
  `mpg`,
  `cyl`,
  `disp`
```
  * `"align"`: each field on its own line. No line break and fields are all aligned
```sql
SELECT `mpg`,
       `cyl`,
       `disp`
```
* **align on AS:**

maybe
* **"AND" position:**
  * `"line_end"`
  * `"line_start"`: it is a bit easier to remove (or comment out) the last condition
```sql
WHERE
  `mpg` > 1 AND
  `cyl` = 6

-- vs

WHERE
  `mpg` > 1
  AND `cyl` = 6
```
* **"comma" position:** same like for "AND"
* **"keyword alignment:**
  * `"left"`
  * `"right"`
```sql
SELECT *
FROM df

-- vs

SELECT *
  FROM df
```
* **truncate strings**: truncate long strings?
* **truncate lists/vectors**

## Select query
``` r
tbl_lazy(mtcars) %>% 
  mutate(mpg = mpg + 1,
         mpg = mpg - 1) %>% 
  filter(
    mpg > 1,
    cyl == 6
  ) %>% 
  group_by(mpg, cyl) %>% 
  summarise(mpg = mean(mpg, na.rm = TRUE))
```

before
```sql
SELECT `mpg`, `cyl`, AVG(`mpg`) AS `mpg`
FROM (SELECT `mpg` - 1.0 AS `mpg`, `cyl`, `disp`, `hp`, `drat`, `wt`, `qsec`, `vs`, `am`, `gear`, `carb`
FROM (SELECT `mpg` + 1.0 AS `mpg`, `cyl`, `disp`, `hp`, `drat`, `wt`, `qsec`, `vs`, `am`, `gear`, `carb`
FROM `df`) `q01`) `q02`
WHERE ((`mpg` > 1.0) AND (`cyl` = 6.0))
GROUP BY `mpg`, `cyl`
```

after
```sql
SELECT
  `mpg`,
  `cyl`,
  AVG(`mpg`) AS `mpg`
FROM (
  SELECT
    `mpg` - 1.0 AS `mpg`,
    `cyl`,
    `disp`,
    `hp`,
    `drat`,
    `wt`,
    `qsec`,
    `vs`,
    `am`,
    `gear`,
    `carb`
  FROM (
    SELECT
      `mpg` + 1.0 AS `mpg`,
      `cyl`,
      `disp`,
      `hp`,
      `drat`,
      `wt`,
      `qsec`,
      `vs`,
      `am`,
      `gear`,
      `carb`
    FROM `df`
  ) `q01`
) `q02`
WHERE
  (`mpg` > 1.0) AND
  (`cyl` = 6.0)
GROUP BY
  `mpg`,
  `cyl`
```

## Union Query
```r
union(
  union(
    tbl_lazy(mtcars) %>% 
      select(mpg, cyl),
    tbl_lazy(mtcars) %>% 
      select(mpg, cyl)
  ),
  tbl_lazy(mtcars) %>% 
    filter(mpg > 1) %>% 
    transmute(mpg = mpg + 1, cyl)
)
```

before

```sql
((SELECT `mpg`, `cyl`
FROM `df`)
UNION
(SELECT `mpg`, `cyl`
FROM `df`))
UNION
(SELECT `mpg` + 1.0 AS `mpg`, `cyl`
FROM `df`
WHERE (`mpg` > 1.0))
```

after

```sql
(
  (
    SELECT
      `mpg`,
      `cyl`
    FROM `df`
  )
  UNION
  (
    SELECT
      `mpg`,
      `cyl`
    FROM `df`
  )
)
UNION
(
  SELECT
    `mpg` + 1.0 AS `mpg`,
    `cyl`
  FROM `df`
  WHERE (`mpg` > 1.0)
)
```

title: Nicer conditional SQL
description:
This slightly improves the SQL translations of `is.na()`, `if()`, `ifelse()`, `if_else()` and `case_when()`

Before

```r
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
translate_sql(ifelse(is.na(x), 0L, 1L))
#> <SQL> CASE WHEN (((`x`) IS NULL)) THEN (0) WHEN NOT(((`x`) IS NULL)) THEN (1) END

translate_sql(case_when(is.na(x) ~ 0L, TRUE ~ 1L))
#> <SQL> CASE
#> WHEN (((`x`) IS NULL)) THEN (0)
#> ELSE (1)
#> END
```

After

```r
library(dbplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
translate_sql(ifelse(is.na(x), 0L, 1L))
#> <SQL> CASE WHEN ((`x` IS NULL)) THEN 0 WHEN NOT ((`x` IS NULL)) THEN 1 END

translate_sql(case_when(is.na(x) ~ 0L, TRUE ~ 1L))
#> <SQL> CASE WHEN ((`x` IS NULL)) THEN 0 ELSE 1 END
```

title: Add pivot_longer()
description:
Closes #532.
After nothing seems to have happened in PR #342 for more than a year I thought it would be best to create a new PR for this.

I tried to support all the features from `tidyr::pivot_longer()` but there are some open questions:

1. `pivot_longer()` in `tidyr` uses S3 dispatch but `build_longer_spec()` and `pivot_longer_spec()` do not. For now, I simply overwrite both these functions which of course is not the way to go. Would you prefer to change both of them to use S3 dispatch as well or should the functions here have different names?
2. The values are not interleaved in the same order as in `tidyr`. Should we a) not care about the order, b) order them explicitly with `arrange()`, or c) add a flag so the user can decide?
3. What if the resulting column is mixed? Use the db default (which is quite nasty for [RSQLite](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/issues/323))? Try to check compatibility locally? Try to coerce similarly to vctrs?
4. Should `values_transform` be supported? This seems quite reasonable to me.
5. Should `values_ptypes` be supported? Here only a subset of ptypes would make sense so I am not sure about this one.
6. There is quite a lot of code copy pasted from tidyr just for the string processing. This is required for the support of the `names_sep` and `names_pattern` argument. How do you want to deal with that?
7. For now, I just copy pasted most of the documentation from `tidyr`. How do you want to handle the documentation?

Example for the generated SQL
```r
pivot_longer(
  memdb_frame(!!!anscombe),
  everything(),
  names_to = c(".value", "set"),
  names_pattern = "(.)(.)"
) %>% 
  show_query()
```

```sql
SELECT '1' AS `set`, `x1` AS `x`, `y1` AS `y`
FROM `dbplyr_148`
UNION ALL
SELECT '2' AS `set`, `x2` AS `x`, `y2` AS `y`
FROM `dbplyr_148`
UNION ALL
SELECT '3' AS `set`, `x3` AS `x`, `y3` AS `y`
FROM `dbplyr_148`
UNION ALL
SELECT '4' AS `set`, `x4` AS `x`, `y4` AS `y`
FROM `dbplyr_148`
```

The generated SQL code is quite a bit shorter than in the other PR as I didn't use `inner_join()`. I don't understand why @edgararuiz used the `inner_join()` so I left it out and it seems to work anyways...

I also checked for the examples in the `pivot_longer()` documentation whether the results match (up to the ordering)

<details>
<summary>
Test with tidyr examples
</summary>

```r
devtools::load_all(".")
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), path = ":dbname:")

relig_income <- tidyr::relig_income
billboard <- tidyr::billboard
who <- tidyr::who


equal_pivot_longer <- function(x, ...) {
  x_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(x, ...) %>% 
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::across(everything()))
  
  y_long <- pivot_longer(
    copy_to(con, x, name = "tmp_table", overwrite = TRUE),
    ...
  ) %>% 
    collect() %>% 
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::across(everything()))
  
  all.equal(
    x_long,
    y_long
  )
}

equal_pivot_longer(
  relig_income,
  !religion, names_to = "income", values_to = "count"
)

equal_pivot_longer(
  billboard %>% mutate(date.entered = as.character(date.entered)),
  cols = starts_with("wk"),
  names_to = "week",
  names_prefix = "wk",
  values_to = "rank",
  values_drop_na = TRUE
)

# Multiple variables stored in column names
equal_pivot_longer(
  who,
  cols = new_sp_m014:newrel_f65,
  names_to = c("diagnosis", "gender", "age"),
  names_pattern = "new_?(.*)_(.)(.*)",
  values_to = "count"
)

# Multiple observations per row
equal_pivot_longer(
  anscombe,
  everything(),
  names_to = c(".value", "set"),
  names_pattern = "(.)(.)"
)
```

</details>

title: add verb `uncount()`
description:
As `uncount()` currently isn't a generic (also see https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/1071) I named the function with `dbplyr_uncount()`.

I see two strategies for translating:

* use a recursive common table expression (see [this stackoverflow discussion](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/33327837/repeat-rows-n-times-according-to-column-value))
* or use an unequal join with a temporary table (the strategy I chose)

The recursive CTE would require much more code and also more testing across backends. Therefore, I simply chose the unequal join. I'm not sure how big the performance difference is.

There are also two variants to create the temporary table

* use the `generate_series()` function. Unfortunately, this is only available as an SQLite extension which is not included in  RSQLite.
* get the maximum value of the weights column and create a local tibble to upload.

The functionality is basically the same as the `tidyr` version with the small difference that the `weights` are not checked as strictly (i.e. no error if some weights are not non-negative integers).

Overview of the strategy:

1. get the max weight, `n_max`
2. create a temporary db table with ids from 1 to `n_max`
3. duplicate data by inner joining with this temporary table under the condition that `data$weight <= tmp$id`

The generated SQL looks like this

```SQL
SELECT `x`,
       `test`
FROM
  (SELECT `x`,
          `n`,
          `test`
   FROM `dbplyr_366` AS `LHS`
   INNER JOIN `dbplyr_367` AS `RHS` ON (`RHS`.`test` <= `LHS`.`n`))
```

One could simplify the SQL a little

``` r
library(DBI)
library(reprex)

                 dbname = "",
                 port = ,

                  UNION ALL

                  UNION ALL

                  UNION ALL

                  UNION ALL

                  UNION ALL

                  UNION ALL

  dbplyr::window_order(yr, mon) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(LG = lag(sales), LD = lead(sales)) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(yr, mon)
```

title: Added lubridate specifics for Oracle
description:
I've supplied the basic changes needed to fully support oracle with the lubridate functions currently supported across all languages. 

Main differences are:

- Forced cast to timestamp for dates to get hour/minute/second - this shouldn't introduce much if any overhead to queries where it already is a timestamp.
- Today is based on sysdate as CURRENT_DATE has a time in oracle (note this will be the current date of the system the database is running on, *not* the date of the NLS settings of the database, this can be changed if it is different to the other SQL variants)
- I've implemented as.Date via an explicit call to Date rather than via a cast - there's 2 reasons for this. The first is that the database optimiser can't identify casts as dates at run time so it might not e.g. identify it should filter on a partition before a join, rather than after. Secondly, the cast to date is NLS setting dependant in Oracle databases; at least in my experience most users will not actually be aware of what this is so the conversion will fail. The method implemented will work for YYYY-MM-DD formats and as as.Date tries YYYY-MM-DD by default this is consistent with the base R method. I do still have the code for the full(ish) version of as.Date/as_date that includes the format argument specific to an Oracle translation however did not include it as the base backend does not support this argument.
- I've also included support for yday and wday as they were listed explicitly in the backend so assumed they would be supported soon and Oracle has a very easy to_char function to extract them.

title: Hive translations for window functions were no more working
description:
This comes from a question on [community.rstudio.com](https://community.rstudio.com/t/error-using-dbplyr-1-4-with-row-number/29779/5)

In dbplyr 1.3.0
```r
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)
tab <- tbl_lazy(iris, src = simulate_hive())
query <- tab %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  filter(row_number() == 1L)
query %>% show_query()
<SQL> SELECT `Sepal.Length`, `Sepal.Width`, `Petal.Length`, `Petal.Width`, `Species`
FROM (SELECT `Sepal.Length`, `Sepal.Width`, `Petal.Length`, `Petal.Width`, `Species`, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY `Species`) AS `zzz1`
FROM `df`) `ohjggmqvbj`
WHERE (`zzz1` = 1)
```
With 1.4.0
```r
tab <- tbl_lazy(iris, src = simulate_hive())
query <- tab %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  filter(row_number() == 1L)
query %>% show_query()
<SQL>
SELECT *
FROM `df`
WHERE (row_number() = 1)
```

A `git bisect` points to this commit: f4fcfdc9f73d56bbf2d93eb705b57709ccae52e5. This comes from a small typo - odbc window function were no more used. 

This PR changes that and now it is working as before
```r
tab <- tbl_lazy(iris, src = simulate_hive())
query <- tab %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  filter(row_number() == 1L)
query %>% show_query()
<SQL>
SELECT `Sepal.Length`, `Sepal.Width`, `Petal.Length`, `Petal.Width`, `Species`
FROM (SELECT `Sepal.Length`, `Sepal.Width`, `Petal.Length`, `Petal.Width`, `Species`, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY `Species`) AS `zzz1`
FROM `df`) `dbplyr_001`
WHERE (`zzz1` = 1)
```

I can add tests later if you want. There are not so many tests for hive curently, and nothing about window function

title: Add main lubridate function support to Oracle
description:
Hi,

I have added as many of the (at least from my experience) key lubridate functions to be translated into Oracle SQL as possible (they may work for other SQL variants but I do not have experience with those). This includes most of the getting and setting functions (those not included are mainly due to Oracle not having those measures and the date math just gets too complex, at least for me), floor/ceiling/round_date, and one or two of the other functions as I needed a break from the bigger ones.

There's currently 5 outstanding issues with the code:
1) I cannot work out how to have round_date call floor/ceiling_date in the same definition, it should be a one liner but I am not sure how to do it.
2) I have had to re-introduce the dependency on stringR to parse the units, again this was because I couldn't work out how to access the function that now does this for the actual lubridate package so took the original parsing code. As the parsing is done R-side it should be able to be removed I again just don't know how.
3) There is little to no support for timestamp datatypes and therefore timezones. Most of the functions have been built explicitly with a call to to_date or date related functions that will not retain timestamp info. In part this was due to trying to keep it simple, and in part due to my lack of experience with Oracle timestamps and timezones. In addition to this, a lot of timestamp info is related to the NLS setting of the particular database which make it very hard to verify via testing.
4) There are very few tests; I've been mostly focused on making sure that the SQL actually returns the same results as a pure lubridate call would, so I have been using a table in a database to compare calls, which means I haven't yet written the actual tests for the SQL text itself into the tests file, but all of my tests are now passing. I have also been unable to use dbtest as I only have access to the Oracle DB though an ROracle connection which is not currently supported. 
5) as.Date() (which has to be defined not using cast as this is NLS setting dependant in Oracle at least) currently doesn't return the expected error it should. I still need to look into this one and do more testing for that function as a whole as the sheer volume of possible combinations mean I kept putting that off.

Finally, sorry for all the commits, it's my first PR so didn't realise I should have made another branch first.

title: Add stringr
description:
Add / improve some `stringr` methods.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/23075542/42978757-a03044ce-8b9c-11e8-9564-bdb2e70096a1.png)


```yaml
- str_length:
    mutate: str_length(fld_character)
    filter: str_length(fld_character) > 1
    summarize: n_distinct(str_length(fld_character))
    group_by: str_length(fld_character)
    arrange: str_length(fld_character)
- str_to_upper:
    mutate: str_to_upper(fld_character)
    filter: str_to_upper(fld_character) %in% c("A","B")
    summarize: n_distinct(str_to_upper(fld_character))
    group_by: str_to_upper(fld_character)
    arrange: str_to_upper(fld_character)
- str_to_lower:
    mutate: str_to_lower(fld_character)
    filter: str_to_lower(fld_character) %in% c("a","b")
    summarize: n_distinct(str_to_lower(fld_character))
    group_by: str_to_lower(fld_character)
    arrange: str_to_lower(fld_character)
- str_detect:
    mutate: str_detect(fld_character, '[A-Z]')
    filter: str_detect(fld_character, '[A-Z]')
    summarize: n_distinct(str_detect(fld_character, '[A-Z]'))
    group_by: str_detect(fld_character, '[A-Z]')
    arrange: str_detect(fld_character, '[A-Z]')
- str_to_title:
    mutate: str_to_title(fld_character)
    filter: str_detect(str_to_title(fld_character), '[A-J]')
    summarize: n_distinct(str_to_title(fld_character))
    group_by: str_to_title(fld_character)
    arrange: str_to_title(fld_character)
- str_replace_all:
    mutate: str_replace_all(fld_character, '[A-J]', '*')
    filter: str_detect(str_replace_all(fld_character, '[A-J]', '*'), '*')
    summarize: n_distinct(str_replace_all(fld_character, '[A-J]', '*'))
    group_by: str_replace_all(fld_character, '[A-J]', '*')
    arrange: str_replace_all(fld_character, '[A-J]', '*')
- str_sub:
    mutate: str_sub(fld_character, 4,8)
    filter: str_detect(str_sub(fld_character, 4,8), '[A-J]')
    summarize: n_distinct(str_sub(fld_character, 4,8))
    group_by: str_sub(fld_character, 4,8)
    arrange: str_sub(fld_character, 4,8)
```

title: Use as.sql() in preference to ident() when composing params into SQL
description:
A number of dbplyr functions, such as several backends' `db_write_table` implementations, use a direct call to `ident` to insure quoting of the destination table name.  For example, from `R/db-postgres.r':
```
sql <- build_sql("INSERT INTO ", ident(table), " VALUES ", sql(values))
```
Unfortunately, `ident` forces its arguments to be quoted as single identifiers, so overrides the effect of `ident_q` or `in_schema`.  (The current tests don't catch the problem because the SQLite code path doesn't do this.)

Since `ident` (and `ident_q`) can take multiple inputs, some of which might or might not be previously marked by the other, it'd be hard to make them idempotent with respect to each other.  An alternative would be using a notional `as.ident` function in place of the call to `ident` when one wants to treat an item  as an identifier that may or may not already be so marked.  In practice, it appears that `as.sql` has the desired semantics, in that it respects `ident_q`, quotes `ident`, and quotes a basic character string as an identifier.

Rather than introduce a new `as.ident`, this PR replaces with `as.sql` direct calls to `ident` that quote parameters being passed through to SQL.  I did confirm, using a Postgres test db, that the change causes `copy_to(con, df, in_schema('schema', 'table'))` to work as expected, rather than failing with an error stating that "schema.table" doesn't exist in the current schema.   I haven't included in the PR a new test that'd catch the current problem, since SQLite can't, and I'm not sure it'd be worth the hoops to detect a backend that could in an arbitrary test environment.

If there're downstream problems cause by using `as.sql`, or if you'd just prefer to have a cleaner separation of concepts, I'd be happy to reimplement in terms of a simple `as.ident` like (untested)
```
as.ident <- function (x) if (inherits(x, 'ident') x else ident(x)
```

Thanks for reviewing, and moreso for the improved schema handling in the current dbplyr.

title: SQL translation - Microsoft Access
description:
### Details

This pull request addresses tidyverse/dplyr#2946 by providing an Access SQL translation. 

This branch was branched from another pull request that is still open, #28, because it required the updated `names_to_as()` function there.

Because of problems with writing tables discussed in error 4 below, this is intended to be the _read-only_ piece of the translation until the write errors can be sorted out. Fixing these errors requires modification to the `odbc` package.

### Known errors

These still need to be addressed or added to the db.rstudio.com page.

1) When joining two tables with the same column names, you have to specify `suffix = c("_x", "_y")` over the default of `suffix = c(".x", ".y")` because a `.` cannot exist in Access column names.

2) `full_join` uses the `coalesce` function in the SQL that it builds. This is not supported in Access so it does not work. There is an alternative of using `IFF(Is.Null(x), y, x)` but the `sql_coalesce()` function in `dbplyr` is not generic and I don't think it ever sees the connection object. That alternative solution would also only work with a max of two tables being "coalesced" at once (probably fine with joins but maybe a limitation elsewhere). 

3) While a translation was provided for `dplyr::coalesce()`, `pmin()` and `pmax()`, they only work when comparing a max of 2 objects. The translations were created using variations of `IIF`, for example `pmin` is ``IIF(`field_name_x` <= `field_name_y`,`field_name_x`,`field_name_y`)`` and I am not sure how to easily generalize this.

4) While working with the database, I discovered three `db_*` functions that don't work, and I rolled my own (rough) versions that do. I've created a Gist with that code [here](https://gist.github.com/DavisVaughan/7d8dd9338afcd5c2eb94d751097f5296) and we can talk about including it too if needed. 

     1. `db_drop_table` - Originally uses `IF EXISTS` if "forcing" the drop is required. Access doesn't support this. Rewrote to ask the user if they want to drop, and require them to specify `force = TRUE` if they do. 

     2. `db_copy_to` - As of now, temporary tables aren't supported in Access, so I had to turn that option off.

     3. `db_write_table` - This is a big one. Already posted [here](https://github.com/rstats-db/odbc/issues/79), but `dbWriteTable()` does not yet work with Access `odbc` connections. Fortunately, I found Hadley's solution for [writing tables to MySQL](https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/blob/master/R/db-mysql.r#L80) and Access can actually do a similar thing!

title: Support chained and expression `$` subsetting
description:
This fixes a regression introduced by #1691.

We rely on nested `$` to translate nested proto fields, which mimics how they're accessed in {RProtoBuf}.

See e.g. https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/standard-sql/protocol-buffers#querying_nested_paths.

{bigrquery} is therefore also affected:

https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/query-protobuf-data#example-queries
